extracted.intended_audience: physicists/geophysicists, magnetic observers, navigators, and scientifically literate readers interested in terrestrial magnetism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for observing, measuring, and mapping terrestrial magnetic phenomena (declination, inclination, intensity), and for organizing magnetic observatories and coordinated observation campaigns. Emphasizes instrument standardization, simultaneous and continuous observations, and reduction to common units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization of instruments across network
rubrics_metrics.description: A net-work of stations, provided with similar instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauss distributed new instruments with instructions; magnetic houses/stations should be provided with similar apparatus so observations admit of direct comparison ('instruments which admit of comparison with one another'). Standardized instruments and instructions are essential for comparable, aggregate datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous observations to distinguish local vs global phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Simultaneous and corresponding observations at different stations to distinguish general terrestrial phenomena from mere local disturbances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make coordinated measurements at specified hours at stations to the east and west of central observatory; simultaneous occurrence of perturbations across stations demonstrates general terrestrial phenomena rather than local causes (Humboldt's comparisons between Berlin, Paris, Freiburg, Kasan, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous/uninterrupted multi-day observation series (observatio perpetua)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous and uninterrupted observations of several days and nights (observatio perpetua) are preferable to single observations of many months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt favored continuous observations (hourly or half-hourly) over several days/nights to capture perturbations and periodic variations; example apparatus: Prony's magnetic telescope for fine angular resolution and night lighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of identical needles for comparative oscillation experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative oscillation measurements should be made with the same needle when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt emphasizes comparing the oscillations of the same needle in different places (e.g., Paris, Havana, Mexico) so that changes reflect local magnetic intensity rather than instrument differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of observations to a common standard unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce oscillations and intensity measurements to the standard of force discovered on the magnetic equator in Northern Peru.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically Humboldt's unit (intensity on Peruvian magnetic equator) was used as the standard; published tables reduce local oscillation counts to that unit so global intensities are comparable (e.g., Paris = 1.348 by that standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: High temporal resolution and precise measurement intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations at short intervals and with high precision (e.g., observations at intervals of 2 1/2 minutes; detection of variations as small as 1/40000th of magnetic intensity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnetic observatories record at fine time resolution (sometimes every 2.5 minutes) and uninterrupted 24-hour series to detect small perturbations and periodic phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global distribution of permanent magnetic observatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish permanent stations in both hemispheres at strategic global locations so the magnetic equator and isodynamic/isoclinic systems can be traced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt recommended permanent stations (Toronto, Cape of Good Hope, Van Diemen's Land, St. Helena, Ceylon, New Holland, etc.) and praises coordinated international establishment of magnetic houses to cover both hemispheres for accessibility and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity and frequency of coordinated campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular coordinated campaigns (e.g., simultaneous observations four times a year; proposals for observations at solstices/equinoxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauss's association conducted simultaneous observations quarterly since 1836; Humboldt had earlier proposed campaigns tied to solstices and equinoxes. Campaign scheduling should be chosen to reveal periodic/secular changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth-controlled observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform some observations at controlled depths below the surface (example: 35 fathoms below surface) to reduce surface thermal effects and local disturbances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt describes making simultaneous observations at a depth (35 fathoms) to help distinguish local thermal surface effects from broader phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of delicate optical and chronometrical instruments for intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement of horizontal magnetic power (intensity) should use delicate optical and chronometrical instruments for superior accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optical and chronometrical methods render horizontal power measurements more accurate than older magnetic determinations; such instruments help map isodynamic lines which are valuable for theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reduction via oscillation counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the number of oscillations of a vertical/horizontal needle in a fixed time as a quantitative metric for magnetic intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt reports oscillation counts (e.g., 245 oscillations in Paris in ten minutes) and reduces those counts to a standard intensity; these counts provide a numeric basis for comparing intensity across locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large, geographically extensive datasets for law discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect observations over wide geographic ranges (many degrees of longitude/latitude) to detect global laws (e.g., intensity increase toward poles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt's and others' observations across 188 degrees of longitude and from 60°N to 12°S allowed discovery of the law that magnetic intensity generally increases from equator to poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network coordination and central leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Central institutions (e.g., Gottingen as center) should coordinate instrument distribution, instructions, and data collection for the network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauss erected apparatus and distributed instruments with instructions; central coordination enables comparable simultaneous observations over a large area (Germany, Sweden, Italy, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority on mean numerical values and quantitative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine mean numerical values and seek quantitative relations (space and time) as a stable element amid oscillatory phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt stresses determination of mean numerical values (averages) across observations as the basis for developing quantitative laws of terrestrial magnetism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hourly/diurnal (horary) variations from secular changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Record and analyze hourly (horary) variations dependent on true time and daily solar position separately from secular (long-term) changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horary variations are apparently governed by the Sun while secular motions (e.g., movement of nodes of magnetic equator) require long-term datasets and comparison across years (examples: declination zero at London 1657 vs Paris 1669).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative geography in interpreting isogonal/isodynamic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Map isogonic (declination), isoclinic (inclination), and isodynamic (intensity) lines and compare their configurations and changes in relation to geography for physical interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt discusses closed oval isogonic systems, relation to magnetic equator, and the practical value of isogonic lines for navigation vs isodynamic lines for theory; mapping aids hypothesis about causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical caution: prefer data-driven hypotheses for underlying causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid premature physical explanations; base inferences on accumulated simultaneous, quantitative observations before ascribing causes (e.g., solar, atmospheric, or internal currents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt repeatedly cautions that ultimate physical causes (thermo-electric surface currents, solar influence, planetary rotation, interior currents) remain speculative until supported by comprehensive observations and mean numerical laws.
